strengths: Addresses important and timely problem: calibration degradation in RL-trained reasoning models, with clear motivation for high-stakes applications
Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 elegantly proves that bounded proper scoring rules jointly incentivize correctness and calibration, with clear distinction from unbounded rules like log-loss
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets (HotpotQA, Big-Math, TriviaQA, SimpleQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA) with both in-domain and out-of-domain assessment
Strong out-of-domain calibration results: RLCR maintains/improves calibration on unseen tasks (ECE 0.46→0.21 on HotpotQA OOD) while RLVR hurts it—this is the paper's strongest contribution
Simple and practical method: straightforward to implement, integrates easily with existing RL pipelines, doesn't require additional models
Thoughtful analysis including validation that reasoning improves calibration (Section 4.5), self-consistency analysis (Section 4.6), and test-time scaling applications
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation, informative figures, and concrete examples throughout
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: fundamental idea of using proper scoring rules for calibration is established; Xu et al. (2024) and Stangel et al. (2025) already applied Brier/log-loss rewards. Main novelty is reasoning-specific application and OOD evaluation, which is incremental
Accuracy-calibration tradeoffs underplayed: HotpotQA accuracy drops 63.0%→62.1%, Big-Math OOD RLCR 50.9% vs RLVR 52.5%. Abstract claim of 'no loss in accuracy' overstates results

Verbalized confidence faithfulness questionable: confidence is just a number 0-1 with no evidence model truly understands it as probability; quality of uncertainty analysis inconsistent (appendix shows both generic and specific); Section 4.5 finds small classifiers can outperform on analysis, suggesting reasoning may not drive calibration gains

Out-of-domain calibration remains poor in absolute terms: ECE still high (0.21-0.25 on OOD); Figure 6b shows models assign high summed confidence to contradictory answers on OOD (sums >>1), limiting practical deployment safety value

Theorem 1 limitations: assumes Bernoulli(p_y) success indicator but true probability is deterministic (0 or 1); characterizes reward incentives not optimization dynamics; gap between theory and practice acknowledged but not addressed

Evaluation methodology concerns: LLM-as-judge (Llama-3.1-8B) without inter-rater agreement; manual answer/confidence extraction could bias results; different prompts for RLCR vs RLVR ('Long RLCR' vs 'Simple Generation'); SFT warmup only for Math creates asymmetry; format reward weight effects unclear
Scalability unknown: limited to 7B Qwen2.5; no computational cost analysis; unclear how method scales to larger models or o1-style reasoning models
Statistical rigor: no error bars or significance tests on main results; results appear from single runs; reproducibility limited by custom extraction pipeline and no code release mentioned

strengths: Addresses an important problem: reasoning models become poorly calibrated after RL training, which matters for high-stakes applications
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 datasets with multiple metrics (accuracy, AUROC, Brier, ECE) and OOD generalization testing
Strong OOD calibration improvements: RLCR maintains accuracy while improving calibration, whereas RLVR degrades OOD calibration
Theoretical result (Theorem 1) correctly characterizes the reward function's incentive properties, particularly the insight about bounded vs. unbounded proper scoring rules
Clear presentation with good examples and figures comparing RLCR vs. RLVR outputs
Practical simplicity: method is straightforward to implement by modifying the reward function
Demonstrates verbalized confidences can be effectively used for test-time scaling
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combining a proper scoring rule with correctness is straightforward; concurrent work (Xu et al. 2024; Stangel et al. 2025) pursues similar ideas, and distinctions are unclear

Overstated theoretical claims: 'no cost in accuracy' claim (Theorem 1) assumes models can learn true success probabilities, but this is not guaranteed during training, and empirical results show accuracy regressions (e.g., 62.1% vs 63.0% on HotPotQA)

Problematic baseline comparison: RLVR is trained without uncertainty reasoning then asked to verbalize confidence at test time via prompt, while RLCR was trained on this task—unfair apples-to-apples comparison
SFT warmup confounds results: SFT+RLCR uses expert-generated analyses from Deepseek-R1, making it unclear if improvements come from RLCR or better in-domain supervised data

Questionable reasoning quality (Section 4.5): classifiers can extract signal from solutions alone at larger scales, suggesting uncertainty analysis may not meaningfully influence confidence; appendix examples show generic or circular analyses
Absolute calibration remains poor: OOD ECE values are 0.21–0.33, and Figure 6b shows confidence sums substantially overconfident OOD, undermining claims about reliability for high-stakes applications
OOD generalization explanation is speculative: four hypotheses offered in Section 4.2 with no strong evidence for any; claims about 'non-stationarity' and 'shared representations' are hand-wavy

Incomplete ablations: no ablation on correctness/calibration reward balance, no systematic exploration of different proper scoring rules, limited analysis of when RLCR helps most (improvements vary widely across datasets)
No statistical significance testing: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-run significance tests despite variation across datasets
Limited model scope: only Qwen2.5-7B evaluated; results on other architectures would strengthen generalizability claims

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Addresses genuine issue that standard RL training improves accuracy but degrades calibration in reasoning models

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 formally shows bounded proper scoring rules enable joint optimization of correctness and calibration, with useful distinction from unbounded rules like log-loss
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets, both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, multiple metrics (ECE, Brier, AUROC), and strong baselines
Strong empirical results: Dramatic in-domain calibration improvements (ECE 0.37→0.03 on HotpotQA) while maintaining accuracy; importantly, improves rather than harms OOD calibration unlike RLVR
Thorough analysis sections: Sections 4.5-4.6 investigate whether reasoning genuinely contributes to calibration and examine confidence consistency—important nuances often overlooked
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed appendix with prompts, hyperparameters, implementation details, and complete experimental setup
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Xu et al. (2024) and Stangel et al. (2025) already apply proper scoring rules for RL calibration; this paper's main contribution is combining with correctness reward and proving joint incentive, making it somewhat incremental

Theorem 1 assumptions need better justification: The Bernoulli(p_y) assumption is somewhat circular (outcome is deterministic once y is predicted); epistemically uncertain predictors may not satisfy this; relationship to LM calibration unclear

Confounding experimental factors: Both RLCR and RLVR use format rewards equally weighted with other terms; unclear how much of the improvement comes from structured output vs. calibration; missing ablation without format reward

Incomplete OOD solution: Absolute ECE values remain high out-of-domain (often >0.2); Figure 6b shows confidence sums exceed 1 OOD indicating persistent overconfidence; some individual OOD datasets show accuracy degradation

SFT warmup workaround undermines claims: Math requires SFT+RLCR for good calibration, suggesting core method has limitations; SFT+RLCR causes catastrophic OOD forgetting; requires external model (Deepseek-R1), reducing method elegance

Concerns about verbalized confidence: Section 4.5 finds analysis classifiers outperform baselines only at smaller scales (0.5B, 1.5B, not 7B), suggesting reasoning may not provide calibration signal when model is capable; undermines claim that 'reasoning improves calibration'
Limited scale: Only 7B Qwen model tested; calibration properties often scale-dependent; unclear how method generalizes to larger models
Narrow test-time scaling evaluation: Only ensemble methods tested; other calibration approaches (temperature scaling, adaptive thresholding) not explored
Dataset limitations: HotpotQA-Modified (paragraph removal) is somewhat artificial; would benefit from naturally-occurring distribution shift evaluation
Missing experimental comparisons: No direct comparison to other recent calibration methods for reasoning models beyond post-hoc approaches mentioned in related work

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine issue of calibration degradation in RL-trained reasoning models, critical for high-stakes applications

Solid theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 rigorously proves that combining correctness rewards with bounded proper scoring rules incentivizes both accuracy and calibration; toy experiment convincingly validates why unbounded scoring rules (log loss) fail

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Diverse benchmarks (HotpotQA, math, factual QA, commonsense), both in/out-of-distribution, multiple calibration metrics, strong baselines, generalization across model families
Substantial practical improvements: In-domain ECE 0.37→0.03 (HotpotQA), 0.26→0.10 (Math); out-of-domain consistency; maintains task accuracy

Thorough ablations and analysis: Clear decomposition of reward vs. prompting components (Section 4.6), confidence self-consistency analysis, test-time improvements via confidence-weighted voting, extensive appendices
Maintains accuracy while improving calibration: Unlike calibration-only baselines that collapse to degenerate solutions, RLCR preserves task performance
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core idea of combining correctness rewards with proper scoring rules is straightforward; concurrent work (Xu et al. 2024, Stangel et al. 2025) explores similar ideas; primary contribution is application to reasoning models

Underexplored design space: No ablation on correctness-Brier weighting (λ=1), no comparison of different bounded scoring rules, format reward not thoroughly evaluated; these choices appear important but lack justification

Out-of-distribution calibration still limited: Absolute ECE values remain high (0.21 averaged OOD, up to 0.46 on individual datasets); SFT+RLCR causes accuracy drops (52.5%→43.8%) requiring prompt fixes; CommonsenseQA spurious alignment issue suggests method may capitalize on dataset artifacts

Insufficient analysis of uncertainty reasoning quality: Limited examination of whether generated analyses capture genuine uncertainty sources; Appendix N shows generic analyses; Section G reveals uncertainty reasoning becomes unhelpful at larger model scales, raising questions about mechanism

Incomplete accuracy-calibration trade-off analysis: While RLCR maintains accuracy, it doesn't improve it; trade-offs emerge (SFT+RLCR) but are underanalyzed; no principled approach to balancing objectives when conflicts arise

Scalability and generalization concerns: Experiments limited to 7-8B models with no larger model evaluation; computational overhead of longer outputs not discussed; limited evaluation beyond QA/math domains

Experimental design confounds: RLCR uses longer prompts with analysis tags vs. RLVR baseline; different initialization for different baselines; statistical significance of some results unclear given overlapping confidence intervals

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical importance for reliable reasoning models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9+ datasets with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution testing
Theoretical analysis of why bounded vs unbounded proper scoring rules matter for RL
Some substantial improvements on specific benchmarks (HotpotQA ECE 0.37→0.03)
Thorough ablations isolating contributions of reward-based optimization vs uncertainty reasoning
Generalization demonstrated across multiple model families (Qwen, OlMo)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Xu et al. (2024) and Stangel et al. (2025) already apply proper scoring rules to RL for calibration; application to reasoning models is incremental
Weak comparison to prior work: Table 6 shows Calibration RL (Analysis+Conf Only) achieves nearly identical results (ECE 0.08 vs 0.03) to RLCR with equal accuracy, undermining claimed advantages
Critical robustness concern: SFT+RLCR variant collapses to 43.8% OOD accuracy; while explained by formatting biases, this raises serious questions about method stability
Absolute out-of-domain calibration remains poor: ECE 0.21 on averaged OOD datasets is substantial; paper acknowledges room for improvement is 'significant'
Theorem 1 is straightforward application of proper scoring rule theory with the Savage-Dawid representation; lacks novel insights into calibration dynamics in RL
Confounded experimental design: format rewards weighted equally with calibration rewards but ablation missing; unclear how much improvement comes from each component

Appendix G reveals concerning result: uncertainty analysis CoTs only improve calibration at small model sizes (0.5B, 1.5B), not at 7B, suggesting uncertainty reasoning may not be meaningfully leveraged by expressive models
Why uncertainty reasoning helps beyond the loss function is unexplored; paper provides hypotheses but no analysis
Non-standard modified HotpotQA dataset hinders comparison to other work; custom dataset choices limit reproducibility
Circular dependency not addressed: models must output calibrated confidences during training to learn calibration—this bootstrapping assumption needs justification

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing hallucination and overconfidence in reasoning models
Strong theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 elegantly proves joint optimization of correctness and calibration, with insightful analysis of why bounded vs. unbounded scoring rules differ

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: diverse datasets (QA, math, commonsense), both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, multiple strong baselines including expensive post-hoc classifiers, ablation studies, cross-model validation
Practical utility demonstrated: shows verbalized confidences improve test-time ensemble methods, analyzes self-consistency, dramatic in-domain improvements (ECE 0.37→0.03 on HotpotQA)
Well-executed empirical work: rigorous methodology, proper statistical reporting, clear writing, thorough appendices supporting reproducibility
Good design choices: toy bandit experiment effectively illustrates log-loss failure, ablations isolate reward function vs. reasoning components, comparisons across model families
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: similar reward combination ideas exist in concurrent work (Xu et al. 2024, Stangel et al. 2025) for non-reasoning tasks; main contribution is application to reasoning models and empirical validation, somewhat incremental

Out-of-distribution calibration remains problematic: while improving over RLVR, absolute ECE/Brier scores still high on OOD tasks, confidence sums exceed 1 indicating persistent overconfidence, insufficient for high-stakes applications (healthcare, law)
No accuracy improvements: maintains in-domain accuracy vs. RLVR but doesn't improve it (62.1% vs 63.0%), with comparable or slightly worse OOD accuracy, limiting overall impact beyond reliability

Uncertain mechanisms: Table 2 and Appendix G show uncertainty reasoning may not be essential (7B classifiers extract similar info from RLVR), mechanistic understanding of what drives improvements is limited, three proposed hypotheses not rigorously tested
SFT+RLCR brittleness: significant OOD accuracy drop (52.5%→43.8%) despite prompt engineering fix, suggests domain-specific overfitting and raises generalization concerns

Evaluation metric limitations: heavy reliance on ECE which has known binning artifacts; missing adaptive ECE, MCE, or cross-entropy reporting; no user studies on practical significance of calibration improvements
Scalability not addressed: all experiments on 7B models, unclear if benefits persist at frontier model scales (70B+), token efficiency overhead (~3x vs RLVR) not deeply analyzed
Dataset-dependent results: improvements vary substantially across benchmarks (GPQA AUROC 0.49→0.55 is modest), all methods overconfident on CommonsenseQA, generality uncertain
